catalog_quote: There are three types of word stress in Kasong: strong stress, weak stress and unstress. The strong stress is always on the major syllable and occurs in every monosyllabic word and on the last syllable of disyllabic and trisyllabic words. It is symbolized by [S] and is marked in phonetic transcription with a raised vertical line, [ ' ]. The weak stress is always on the minor syllable of disyllabic words. It may be on the first syllable of trisyllabic word type 1 or the second syllable of trisyllabic word type 2. It is symbolized by [W] and is marked by [, ] in the phonetic transcription. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable and word-final: the primary ('strong') stress falls on the major syllable, which is the only syllable of a monosyllable and the last syllable of every di- and trisyllabic word; non-final syllables are either weakly stressed 'minor' syllables (closed CVC, neutral pitch) or unstressed 'presyllables' (Ca, neutral pitch). Lexical pitch/register contrasts (4 registers) are realised on the stressed major syllable only.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A 'weak stress' [,] is assigned to minor syllables (CVC non-final syllables, e.g. [,sam.'khu:n] 'woman', [,tok.ka.'ho:k] 'to snore'); presyllables (Ca) are fully unstressed (e.g. [ka.'mo:] 'stone'). Ploykaew 2001 (Samre Grammar sec. 2.3.3) describes the same three-degree system for Samre of Trat, with secondary stress on non-final full syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: None to the final-stress rule. Only two native trisyllabic words exist ([,tok.ka.'ho:k] 'to snore', [ka.,tcho:p.'lo:h] 'cramp'), both final-stressed; 55% of tested vocabulary is Thai loans (abstract), not said to behave differently. Ploykaew 2001:34 notes Thai-loan trisyllables in Samre are likewise final-stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (chapter V 'The Phonological Word' in a Pike-style hierarchy intonation group > phonological word > syllable > phoneme); forms are citation/elicited words. Stress is declared predictable and non-phonemic (5.3.4). The language is a register language (4 registers = pitch x clear/breathy on the major syllable; 'pitch in Kasong is unpredictable', 5.4) said to be developing into a tone language; presyllable/minor-syllable pitch is neutral and non-contrastive (5.4.2). Corroborated for the same lect by Kamnuansin 2002:11 ('only one main stress which occurs on the major syllable at the end of word') and for the co-member lect Samre of Trat by Ploykaew 2001 MKS 31:17 and Samre Grammar pp.32-35 ('The primary stress always falls on the last syllable').
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog cent2314 'Central Chong' (no ISO; = Sidwell 2009's Central Chong node) bundles two Pearic lects of Bo Rai district, Trat, Thailand: (a) Kasong, autonym of the 'Chong of Trat' of Khlong Saeng / Dan Chumphon sub-district (Isarangura 1935, Kunwadee 1996, Kamnuansin 2002/2003, Thongkham 2003; Glottolog links cent2314 to ELP 'Kasong'), and (b) the 'Samre' of Ban Mamuang, Tambon Nonsi (Thongkum 1984, Ploykaew 2001; Glottolog ref 32798 language code 'Samre.. = Central Chong'). The quoted statement is from the dedicated Kasong phonology (Thongkham 2003); Ploykaew 2001 states the identical rule for Samre of Trat, so the reading holds for both member lects. Speakers and Suwilai (2001) regard Kasong and Samre as different languages. Do not confuse with chon1284 Chong of Chanthaburi [cog] (DiCanio, Huffman, Choosri) or with Cambodian Somray/Samre (somr1240; retired samr1245, where our catalog earlier refused to attach Ploykaew 2001).

sources.note: Sec. 5.3 Word Stress (pp.42-44): three degrees (strong, weak, unstress); strong stress always on the major syllable = every monosyllable and the last syllable of di- and trisyllabic words; weak stress on minor (CVC) syllables, unstress on presyllables; 5.3.4: stress predictable, not written phonemically. Sec. 5.4: pitch of presyllables/minor syllables neutral; 4 registers on major syllable; abstract: Kasong developing into a tone language.
